title: "Number of ratings, rater differences, and score reliability in creativity ratings of football actions: A judge response theory analysis"
shorttitle: "Rater differences and reliability in creativity ratings of football actions"
author:

abstract: |
  The consensual assessment technique (CAT) is the standard procedure for rating the creativity of products and is increasingly applied to actions in sport. However, it is unknown how many ratings an action needs for a reliable creativity score, and how much raters differ when they judge creativity in sport. In this exploratory study, 19 raters provided 7820 ratings of 3668 football actions on a 7-point creativity scale. Judge response theory models were fitted by marginal maximum likelihood: a graded response model (GRM) was compared with an adjacent-category ladder ranging from the many-facet Rasch model to the generalized partial credit model. The empirical reliability of the obtained scores was 0.672 [0.649, 0.687], against 0.960 for a hypothetical full panel. Mean product-level reliability rose from 0.520 with one rating to 0.698 with two and 0.810 with four ratings. Rater discrimination ranged from 0.631 to 3.709, and the most lenient and most severe first thresholds were -6.565 and 0.295. Likelihood-ratio tests rejected a shared category structure and equal discrimination (both *p* < .001). Scoring actions by their raw mean rating placed a share of 0.350 of actions in a different quintile than the GRM scores; the many-facet Rasch model did so for 0.202. These results suggest that creativity studies in sport should plan the number of ratings per action, link raters through a common calibration set, and model rater differences rather than average them. # Introduction

Creativity is widely regarded as one of the core competencies of the modern world. Employers rank creative thinking among the core skills of the workforce [@worldeconomicforum2025] [\[FILL IN: verify this wording against the report; also verify the framing claims attributed to safardilha2019, memmert2011, batey2012 and barbot2019b against the PDFs (FI-17)\]]{.mark}, and the Programme for International Student Assessment assessed creative thinking as an innovative domain in its 2022 cycle [@oecd2024]. In sport, creativity is considered a key quality to be developed and evaluated in players [@safardilha2019; @santos2016]. Assessing creativity validly and reliably is therefore a basic task, in society in general and in sport in particular.

Creativity research distinguishes four facets of creativity: the creative person, the creative process, the creative product and the press, that is, the environment in which creativity occurs [@batey2012]. Each facet requires its own measurement approach [@barbot2019; @barbot2019b]. The present paper is concerned with the product facet, namely actions performed in football matches, and with the evaluation of these actions by others.

The consensual assessment technique (CAT) is the established method for evaluating creative products [@amabile1982; @hennessey2011; @kaufman2024]. In the CAT literature and in judge response theory, raters are called judges; we use "raters" throughout. In the CAT, raters who are familiar with the domain rate products independently and relative to one another [@amabile1982; @hennessey2011]. Although the procedure rests on subjective judgements, independent raters usually reach coefficient alphas above .70 [@baer2004; @kaufman2008; @hennessey2011]. Considerably lower agreement has also been reported, however, and has been attributed to differences between raters in rating procedure, in their use of the rating scale and in their beliefs about creativity [@long2015; @cseh2019].

The reliability of CAT scores rests on the number of raters. As already noted by @amabile1982, the Spearman–Brown reliability of an aggregated rating depends jointly on the mean inter-rater correlation and on the number of raters, so that a larger panel compensates for lower agreement between individual raters. Conversely, a high alpha obtained from a large panel can mask low agreement among individual raters [@kaufman2008]. A rule of thumb of five to ten raters is often cited [@kaufman2008a], but @cseh2019 argue that the number of raters needed depends on the product and the domain and must therefore be established empirically for each domain. A further distinction becomes important when many products are rated. A panel coefficient describes the mean over all raters of the panel. When each product receives only some of the possible ratings, what matters for the use of a score is the precision of each product's score given the ratings that this product actually received [@primi2019; @forthmann2023].

Raters also differ systematically. They differ in severity, in their use of the rating scale and in their beliefs about creativity [@long2015], and their tendencies can drift over time [@barth2020]. Research on rater-mediated assessment has described these differences as rater effects, including severity, central tendency, restriction of range and halo [@engelhard1994; @myford2003; @myford2004]. In judged sports, the accuracy and bias of competition officials have been monitored with Rasch-family or other statistical models, although for performance quality rather than for creativity [@looney2004; @anderlucci2021; @heiniger2021].

How such rater differences are handled depends on the scoring model, and the development from averaging to judge response theory (JRT) can be described as a successive relaxation of assumptions about raters. Mean scores and coefficient alpha treat raters as interchangeable, (essentially) $\tau$-equivalent measures of the same attribute [@myszkowski2019]. Whenever different raters rate different products, mean scores are confounded with the severity of the raters who happened to rate each product [@primi2019]. Item response theory (IRT) instead models the probability of each response as a function of a latent attribute and of item parameters [@lord1980; @embretson2013; @deayala2022]. Rasch models constrain all items to discriminate equally [@rasch1960; @bond2020]; their polytomous extensions, the rating scale model [RSM, @andrich1978] and the partial credit model [PCM, @masters1982], differ in whether all items share one category structure. The many-facet Rasch model (MFRM) adds rater severity as an additive facet [@linacre1989; @eckes2015] and has been applied to creativity ratings by @primi2019. It retains equal discrimination, however, so that differences in discrimination have no parameter and surface only as misfit [@myford2004; @myszkowski2021]. JRT treats raters as items with their own discrimination and thresholds, for instance in the generalized partial credit model [GPCM, @muraki1992] or the graded response model [GRM, @samejima1969], and yields scores with product-specific standard errors as well as an explicit description of rater behaviour [@myszkowski2019; @myszkowski2021]. JRT has been applied in recent creativity research [@barbot2023; @pellegrino2025], and @pellegrino2025 retained a GRM; simulation work has addressed planned-missing rating designs [@forthmann2023]. Two model families are available. The RSM, PCM and GPCM are adjacent-category models and nested, so that their constraints can be tested by likelihood-ratio tests. The GRM is a cumulative model, which arguably matches a scale on which raters express an increasing amount of creativity [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-8\]]{.mark}; the two families can be compared by information criteria.

Creativity research in sport has focused mainly on the creative process, for example on divergent thinking [@memmert2011]. Ratings of creative products, that is, of actions, exist as well. @kempe2018 obtained ratings of actions in competition from trained experts and found face validity in the proximity of the rated actions to goals; their scale originated in expert ratings of tactical creativity [@memmert2007]. Further studies have rated football actions [@zahno2023; @dejoode2023]. These studies average the ratings and report intraclass correlations or agreement at most; a Rasch validation exists only for a coach-completed creativity questionnaire that rates players rather than actions [@shin2025]. However, three gaps remain. First, there is no evidence on how many ratings per action are needed for a reliable creativity score in sport, which is the domain-specific evidence called for by @cseh2019. Second, there is no evidence on how raters differ when they judge the creativity of sport actions. Third, to our knowledge, no study has modelled such rater differences with IRT or JRT for creativity ratings in sport. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-2: the literature search was not systematic\]]{.mark}

## The present study

The present study analysed a large set of CAT-style creativity ratings of football actions given by multiple raters (see Methods and @tbl-design-summary). The study was exploratory and had three aims: (1) to describe how the reliability of creativity scores depends on the number of ratings, (2) to describe how raters differ, and (3) to examine whether these rater differences need to be modelled. No confirmatory hypotheses were formulated; the following research questions (RQs) were answered descriptively. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-20: exploratory framing and RQ wording\]]{.mark}

- **RQ1 (number of ratings and reliability).** How does the reliability of creativity scores depend on the number of ratings per product (i.e., per action)? How does the reliability of the scores actually obtained compare with the reliability of a hypothetical full panel and with conventional agreement and consistency indices?
- **RQ2 (rater differences).** How do raters differ in their rating behaviour, that is, in severity, scale use, discrimination and their contribution to information, and how precisely are these differences estimated?
- **RQ3 (modelling rater differences).** (a) Are the constraints that treat raters as equivalent, namely a shared category structure and equal discrimination, tenable for these ratings? (b) How far do product scores and rankings change when rater differences are ignored (raw mean ratings) or constrained (MFRM/RSM, PCM, GPCM)?

Two secondary questions concerned the scoring model: which model describes the ratings best, and what fit evidence is available for it (SQ1), and how strongly the product scores depend on the choice of model (SQ2). To answer these questions, we fitted a ladder of JRT models and a GRM by marginal maximum likelihood, estimated the reliability of the scores actually obtained, described the rater parameters with their uncertainty, and compared GRM scores with raw mean ratings. Rater expertise and the design of the rating scale are outside the scope of this paper.

# Methods

## Overview and study context

This was a CAT-style rating study in which raters independently rated the creativity of football actions in a randomised order [@amabile1982; @hennessey2011]. The ratings were collected as part of a larger project. [\[FILL IN: context and purpose of the larger project (FI-1, FI-2)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: ethics approval (committee, reference number) and informed-consent procedure (FI-1)\]]{.mark} The analyses reported here were exploratory. [\[FILL IN: preregistration status, e.g., a statement that the study was not preregistered (FI-15)\]]{.mark}

## Raters

Raters were Bachelor's and Master's students who rated actions as part of their thesis projects. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; FI-1\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: recruitment, number of raters at the start, demographics, football playing or coaching experience and compensation, or a statement that these were not recorded (FI-1)\]]{.mark} The final data comprised 19 raters, who gave between 50 and 1174 ratings each (@tbl-design-summary). Raters were pseudonymised as R01 to R19; the three excluded raters (see Data preparation and final data) are R20 to R22.

## Products and stimulus material

Each rated product was a single football action. Actions were shown as video clips from recorded football matches and were identified with event data. [\[FILL IN: competitions and matches (the project notes mention FIFA, AFCON, UEFA and Copa América matches with StatsBomb event data; to be verified), the action-selection rule, clip length, video source and number of matches (FI-2)\]]{.mark}

## Rating procedure

[\[FILL IN: rating software (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Raters were shown an instruction that defined creativity as the combination of originality and functionality of an action in its game context [@runco2012]. [\[FILL IN: verbatim instruction and creativity definition, original language and English translation (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Showing a definition departs to a minor degree from the CAT rule that raters receive no criteria [@hennessey2011], and resembles the procedure of trained-rater studies in sport [@kempe2018; @memmert2007]. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-19\]]{.mark} Creativity was rated on a unipolar 7-point scale with verbal anchors at 1, 4 and 7. [\[FILL IN: verify the anchors and give their wording (FI-3)\]]{.mark} In addition, raters could mark an action as not recognised. [\[FILL IN: wording of the "not recognised" option (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Actions were presented in a randomised order. [\[FILL IN: randomisation procedure, session length and breaks, data-collection period (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Raters also rated technical correctness and aesthetic appeal, which are not analysed here. [\[FILL IN: wording and scales of the other rated dimensions (FI-3)\]]{.mark}

## Rating design

[\[FILL IN: how products were allocated to raters, including planned overlap between raters, any common or benchmark set, randomisation, and how the additional ratings will be allocated (FI-4)\]]{.mark} Not every rater rated every product. The design was therefore incomplete but connected: all raters and products formed a single connected component, so that all rater parameters and product scores could be placed on one scale (@tbl-design-summary). Marginal maximum likelihood estimation assumes that the missing ratings are missing at random given the design. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-18: if a planned benchmark set rated by all raters was not realised as a fully crossed block, state this here\]]{.mark}

## Data preparation and final data

The raw export contained 9148 rows. The 1290 ratings marked 'action not recognised' were removed; such ratings result from video cutting and imperfect material, where close-ups or other TV artefacts render the action non-visible. One out-of-range value (0.0, given by R04) was removed. Twelve rater–product pairs had been entered more than once, one of them with conflicting values; for each pair, the last entry was kept, which removed 13 rows. This left 7844 ratings by 22 raters.

Three raters gave fewer than 15 ratings: R20 (13 ratings), R21 (9) and R22 (2), together 24 ratings (@tbl-excluded-raters). Raters with fewer than 15 ratings were excluded because their up to seven rater-specific parameters cannot be estimated reliably; excluding them did not change the scores (see supplement). The refit with all raters is reported in @tbl-sensitivity-rater-exclusion and summarised in the Results. One product that had been rated only by the excluded raters was dropped.

@tbl-design-summary describes the final data on which all models were fitted: 7820 ratings of 3668 products by 19 raters. Ratings were given on the scale 1–7 and coded 0–6 internally. Products received a mean of 2.132 ratings (median 2, range 1–10, harmonic mean 1.726). The product-by-rater matrix had a fill of 0.112 and formed one connected component; 17 of the 171 rater pairs had no product in common, and the median overlap between rater pairs was 13 products. The distribution of the number of ratings per product is shown in @fig-overview-degree-distributions.

Five raters left categories at the top of the scale unused: category 7 was never used by R01, R03, R06 and R18, and categories 6 and 7 were never used by R17 (@tbl-category-usage). No rater left a category inside their observed range unused. Because the models estimate thresholds only between categories that a rater actually used, these raters have fewer thresholds.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-design-summary >}}

## Measurement models

All models share the JRT frame [@myszkowski2019; @myszkowski2021]. Raters take the role of items and products the role of persons, and the creativity of products is a single latent dimension $\theta$ with a standard normal distribution. A rater's severity is expressed by the location of their thresholds, with higher thresholds indicating a stricter rater; their scale use is expressed by the spacing of the thresholds; and their discrimination $a$ expresses how sharply their ratings separate products of different creativity.

The adjacent-category ladder comprised three nested models. M1 was the RSM [@andrich1978], which is equivalent to a two-facet MFRM with products and raters as facets [@linacre1989; @eckes2015; @primi2019]; it gives each rater a severity but assumes a shared category structure and equal discrimination. M1 was estimated with `sirt::rm.facets` [@robitzsch2025]. M2 was the PCM [@masters1982], which gives each rater their own thresholds, and M3 was the GPCM [@muraki1992], which additionally gives each rater their own discrimination. M2 and M3 were estimated with the R package mirt [@chalmers2012].

The retained scoring model was a GRM with rater-specific discriminations and thresholds [@samejima1969], also estimated in mirt. Its thresholds are ordered by construction. The GRM was estimated by marginal maximum likelihood with the EM algorithm and 61 quadrature points; standard errors were obtained with Oakes' identity [@chalmers2018]. The model converged after 165 iterations, and the information matrix was positive definite (@tbl-grm-convergence). [\[FILL IN: convergence tolerance, which is displayed as 0.000 in the table (FI-6)\]]{.mark}

## Model comparison

Within the nested ladder, two likelihood-ratio (LR) tests were computed: M1 versus M2 tested rater-specific thresholds, and M2 versus M3 tested rater-specific discriminations. For all four models, the log-likelihood, the Akaike (AIC) and Bayesian (BIC) information criteria and the sample-size adjusted BIC (SABIC) were computed, together with the difference to the best model on each criterion. Because the GRM and the ladder belong to different families and are not nested, the GRM was compared with the ladder by information criteria only.

Two features of this comparison need to be noted. First, the M1–M2 test compares models estimated in different software (sirt and mirt). Second, its degrees of freedom are below the formula value. The formula $(J-1)(K-2)$, with $J$ raters and $K$ categories, assumes that every rater used all seven categories. A rater who never used an end category has one step parameter fewer in M2, so the observed degrees of freedom are smaller by the number of unused end categories, which are listed per rater in @tbl-category-usage.

## Model adequacy

Model adequacy was examined with three rater-level statistics and one global statistic. Infit and outfit mean squares [@wright1982] were computed for each rater under M1 and under the GRM. Their expected value is 1, and no misfit cut-offs were applied. With about two ratings per product, values below 1 are expected, because each product's score is estimated from the very ratings being checked. The S-X² item-fit statistic [@orlando2000; @kang2008] requires complete data; the missing ratings were therefore imputed 20 times from the fitted model, and the statistic was averaged over the imputations. Because about 90% of the cells were imputed, this test is conservative.

Local dependence was examined with Yen's Q3 [@yen1984], the correlation of two raters' residuals over the products both rated. Because Q3 is negatively biased when few raters rate each product [@christensen2017], rater pairs were compared by the deviation of their Q3 from the mean Q3 over all computable pairs. A pair was flagged when it had at least 30 jointly rated products and its Q3 deviated from the mean Q3 by more than 0.2.

Global fit was to be assessed with the limited-information statistic C2 [@cai2014]. C2 could not be computed: it needs the joint distribution of every rater pair, which is undefined for the 17 of 171 rater pairs that share no products.

## Scores and reliability

Product scores were expected a posteriori (EAP) estimates $\hat\theta$, with the posterior standard deviation (PSD) as their conditional standard error. The primary reliability index was the empirical marginal reliability, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) / [\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) + \overline{\mathrm{PSD}^2}]$, which refers to the scores actually obtained. For comparison, the model-based marginal reliability [@green1984] was computed with mirt; it refers to a hypothetical product rated by all raters. A computation on a grid of $\theta$ values served as a check.

Ninety-five percent intervals for both reliabilities were obtained from 200 accepted draws of the model parameters from their asymptotic normal distribution, defined by the estimates and the Oakes covariance matrix. For the empirical reliability, products were also resampled in each draw. A draw was rejected and replaced when it did not define a valid GRM, that is, when some discrimination was $\leq 0$ or some rater's thresholds were out of order; 87 draws were rejected and replaced.

At the product level, two reliability indices were computed. The posterior-based index was rel~post~ $= 1 - \mathrm{PSD}^2$. The information-based index was rel~info~ $= I/(I+1)$, where $I$ is the information that the product's own raters provide at its $\hat\theta$. The agreement of the two indices served as a consistency check, and both were summarised by the number of ratings per product.

As reference values for common practice, which were not used in any further analysis, three conventional indices were computed. Cronbach's alpha [@cronbach1951] was computed from pairwise covariances over all usable raters and, alternatively, on the largest fully crossed block of raters and products. [\[FILL IN: why five raters (R19, R14, R02, R16, R12) were not usable for the pairwise alpha; optionally, which three raters form the crossed block (FI-9)\]]{.mark} Krippendorff's ordinal alpha [@hayes2007] measured the agreement of single ratings. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals were obtained by bootstrapping products (1000 replications). For the pairwise Cronbach's alpha, replications in which some rater pair lost all shared products could not be computed; 361 of the 1000 replications failed, and the interval, which is therefore approximate, is based on the remaining replications. On the choice of reliability indices in incomplete rating designs, see @tenhove2024.

## Rater parameters, information and response styles

For each rater, the GRM discrimination $a$ and thresholds $b_k$ were reported with their standard errors. Rater information was integrated over the standard normal distribution of $\theta$, which gives the average information per rating. Each rater's share of the information of the full panel was computed both as a weighted share over $\theta$ and at selected values of $\theta$. Ninety-five percent intervals for information and shares were obtained from the same parameter draws as the reliability intervals.

Descriptive response styles were computed on the raw 1–7 scale: each rater's mean, standard deviation, number of categories used, entropy (natural logarithm), floor rate (share of ratings of 1), ceiling rate (share of ratings of 7), extreme rate (ratings of 1 or 7) and central rate (ratings of 3–5). These descriptives are not adjusted for which products each rater saw.

## Score agreement and sensitivity

To examine RQ3(b), each product's raw mean rating, the common-practice score that treats raters as interchangeable, was compared with its GRM score, overall and by the number of ratings per product (1, 2, 3 or more). The comparison comprised Pearson and Spearman correlations, the absolute shift in percentile rank (on a 0–1 scale), the share of products changing quintile and changing by two or more quintiles, and the mean and maximum range of GRM scores among products with the same raw mean. [\[FILL IN: whether percentiles and quintiles in the 1 / 2 / 3+ groups were computed within each group or over all products, and how the groups of equal raw mean were formed and how many and how large they are (FI-20)\]]{.mark}

To examine SQ2, the EAP scores of all models were correlated (Pearson and Spearman). Relative to the GRM, the absolute shift in percentile rank and the shares of products changing quintile and changing by two or more quintiles were computed. M1 was additionally re-estimated with the default integration grid of sirt as a check. Finally, the sensitivity of the GRM results to the rater exclusion was examined by refitting the GRM with all 22 raters.

## Software and availability

All models were estimated in R with the packages mirt [@chalmers2012] and sirt [@robitzsch2025]; psych and a Krippendorff package were used for the conventional indices, and Python was used for display. [\[FILL IN: versions of R, mirt, sirt, psych and the Krippendorff package (FI-6)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: data and code availability statement; only pseudonymised rater IDs are shared (FI-15)\]]{.mark}

# Results

As outlined in the Introduction, the analyses addressed three aims: the dependence of score reliability on the number of ratings, the differences between raters, and whether these differences need to be modelled. All analyses used the final data in @tbl-design-summary. In summary, the GRM was retained as the scoring model; the reliability of the scores actually obtained was below that of a hypothetical full panel and rose with the number of ratings per product; raters were heterogeneous in all parameters; and the constraints that treat raters as equivalent were rejected, while raw mean ratings ranked products differently from GRM scores.

## Scoring model

As can be seen in @tbl-model-fit, the GRM had the lowest AIC (23720.455), BIC (24508.795) and SABIC (24105.251) of the four models. M3 was 46.566 above the GRM on all three criteria; M2 was 132.524 above it on AIC, 20.790 on BIC and 77.985 on SABIC; and M1 was 701.980, 68.825 and 392.931 above it. The GRM and M3 have the same number of parameters (127), so that their comparison reduces to the log-likelihood, which was $-11733.227$ for the GRM and $-11756.510$ for M3. The GRM converged after 165 EM iterations with a positive definite information matrix (@tbl-grm-convergence).

The rater-level fit statistics of the GRM are given in @tbl-grm-rater-fit. S-X² *p*-values ranged from 0.294 (R12) to 0.671 (R02). Infit ranged from 0.334 (R19) to 0.971 (R18) and outfit from 0.322 (R19) to 0.961 (R18); all values were below 1. The mean Q3 over 137 computable rater pairs was $-0.238$, and 20 pairs were flagged. @tbl-grm-q3-flagged shows the 10 of the 20 flagged pairs with the largest deviation from the mean Q3; nine of them deviated negatively and one (R10–R11) positively. C2 could not be computed (see Model adequacy). As described in the Methods, the informative value of these statistics is limited by the design.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-model-fit >}}

## Number of ratings and reliability of the creativity scores

The reliability of the product scores is summarised by the number of ratings per product in @tbl-grm-reliability-by-n and @fig-grm-rel-post-by-n. Mean rel~post~ rose with each additional rating: it was 0.520 for products with one rating, 0.698 with two, 0.757 with three, 0.810 with four, 0.820 with five, 0.847 with six, 0.869 with seven, 0.875 with eight, 0.879 with nine and 0.919 with ten ratings. Correspondingly, the mean PSD fell from 0.686 to 0.285. The information-based rel~info~ closely tracked rel~post~, with means from 0.544 for one rating to 0.917 for ten ratings. No number of ratings reached a mean rel~post~ as high as the model-based full-panel value of 0.960. As @fig-grm-rel-post-by-n shows, products with the same number of ratings also differed in rel~post~; the relation of rel~post~ to the products' $\hat\theta$ is shown in @fig-grm-rel-post-by-theta.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-grm-reliability-by-n >}}

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#fig-grm-rel-post-by-n >}}

Across all products, rel~post~ had a median of 0.698 and an interquartile range of 0.173 (Q1 0.596, Q3 0.769); the 10th and 90th percentiles were 0.485 and 0.813, and the values ranged from 0.057 to 0.929 (@tbl-grm-reliability-summary; @fig-grm-rel-post-histogram). The two product-level indices agreed closely: they correlated at 0.935, rel~info~ exceeded rel~post~ by 0.016 on average, the largest absolute difference was 0.413, and 320 products differed by more than 0.1 (@fig-grm-rel-consistency).

@tbl-reliability-overview contrasts the indices and states what each refers to. The empirical marginal reliability of the scores actually obtained was 0.672 [0.649, 0.687]. The model-based marginal reliability, which refers to a hypothetical product rated by all raters, was 0.960 [0.953, 0.968], with a grid check of 0.960 (@tbl-grm-reliability-ci; @fig-grm-panel-information). Of the conventional indices, Cronbach's alpha from pairwise covariances was 0.928 [0.891, 0.943] (14 raters, 1900 products); this interval is approximate, because 361 of 1000 bootstrap replications failed (@tbl-naive-indices). On the fully crossed block, Cronbach's alpha was 0.658 [0.526, 0.756] (3 raters, 139 products). Krippendorff's ordinal alpha, which refers to the agreement of single ratings, was 0.392 [0.362, 0.417] (19 raters, 2771 products).

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-reliability-overview >}}

Three qualifications apply to these results. The means by number of ratings have no confidence intervals; the rows for nine and ten ratings rest on three products each; and the comparison across numbers of ratings is observational, because products were not randomly assigned a number of ratings.

## Rater differences

@fig-overview-rater-response-styles gives a descriptive first view of the raters on the raw scale, not adjusted for which products each rater saw. Rater means ranged from 1.760 (R06) to 3.836 (R18), and standard deviations from 1.022 (R01) to 1.953 (R19). Entropy ranged from 1.191 (R06) to 1.903 (R09). The floor rate ranged from 0.579 (R06) to 0.016 (R13). The ceiling rate was highest for R19 (0.080), and five raters (R06, R17, R01, R03 and R18) had a ceiling rate of 0.000. The central rate (ratings of 3–5) was high for R13 (0.799), R18 (0.764) and R12 (0.735) and low for R06 (0.192). Across all ratings, the ratings concentrated at the low end of the scale, with shares of 0.259463 for category 1 and 0.270205 for category 2, whereas category 7 was the rarest (0.013939; @fig-overview-rating-distribution). As noted in the Methods, five raters left top categories unused.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/01_data_overview.ipynb#fig-overview-rater-response-styles >}}

The GRM parameters in @tbl-grm-rater-parameters show these differences on the latent scale, together with their standard errors. First thresholds $b_1$ ranged from $-6.565$ (R18, *SE* 3.047) to 0.295 (R06, *SE* 0.058); R06 was the only rater with a positive first threshold. The spacing of the thresholds also differed: it was narrow for R19 ($b_1 = -0.938$ to $b_6 = 1.692$) and R02 ($-0.706$ to 2.030) and wide for R13 ($-3.384$ to 4.435) and R18 ($b_1 = -6.565$ to $b_5 = 4.440$). R17 had four thresholds, R01, R03, R06 and R18 had five, and all other raters had six. The category response functions are shown in @fig-grm-category-response-functions.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-grm-rater-parameters >}}

Discriminations ranged from 0.631 (R18, *SE* 0.263) to 3.709 (R19, *SE* 2.220); the second highest was that of R16, 3.701 (*SE* 1.359). Raters with many ratings, whose discriminations were estimated more precisely, also differed: R09 had a discrimination of 0.863 (*SE* 0.151), R13 1.504 (*SE* 0.223), R01 1.956 (*SE* 0.159), R02 2.498 (*SE* 0.331) and R06 2.807 (*SE* 0.424).

The average information per rating and each rater's share of the full-panel information are given with 95% intervals in @tbl-grm-rater-information-ci. Information per rating ranged from 0.123 [0.008, 0.352] (R18) to 3.539 [0.410, 11.017] (R19). It was 3.300 [0.728, 6.489] for R16, 0.238 [0.110, 0.419] for R09 and 0.979 [0.723, 1.219] for R01. The corresponding shares were 0.135 [0.017, 0.331] for R19, 0.126 [0.026, 0.223] for R16, 0.037 [0.022, 0.050] for R01 and 0.005 [0.000, 0.013] for R18. Wide intervals indicate that a rater's informativeness is not yet well determined; they occurred typically for raters with few ratings.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-grm-rater-information-ci >}}

Raters also provided information in different regions of the latent scale (@fig-grm-rater-information; @tbl-grm-information-summary). The location of maximum information ranged from 2.700 (R01) and 2.400 (R06) to $-0.550$ (R13). Shares of the panel information varied with $\theta$ (@fig-grm-information-shares): R06 contributed a share of 0.001 at $\theta = -2$ but 0.083 at $\theta = +2$, whereas R12 contributed 0.221 at $\theta = -2$.

The intervals for information and shares rest on the same 200 accepted parameter draws as the reliability intervals. The raw response-style indices, in contrast, have no per-rater uncertainty.

## Modelling rater differences: constraints, raw means and score consequences

The constraints that treat raters as equivalent were examined first. A shared category structure was rejected: the LR test of M1 against M2 gave $\chi^2(84) = 737.457$, *p* < .001 (exact *p* = 4.22e-105; @tbl-lr-tests). Equal discrimination was also rejected: M2 against M3 gave $\chi^2(18) = 121.958$, *p* < .001 (exact *p* = 1.79e-17). AIC also favoured M3 over M2 (23767.020 vs. 23852.978), whereas BIC ranked M2 (24529.585) below M3 (24555.360) (@tbl-model-fit). Rater-specific discriminations were supported by the LR test and AIC, but not by BIC.

Three further results describe the constrained models. Under M3, discriminations ranged from 0.283 (R09, *SE* 0.055) to 2.606 (R16, *SE* 1.419) (@tbl-discrimination-m3). Nine raters had unordered step parameters under M2, and nine under M3 (@tbl-threshold-order); the GRM thresholds are ordered by construction. Under M1, only R17 (infit 1.328, outfit 1.190) and R18 (infit 1.009, outfit 1.071) had values at or above 1, and R12 had the lowest values (infit 0.238, outfit 0.255; @tbl-rater-fit-m1).

The consequences of ignoring rater differences altogether are shown in @tbl-raw-mean-vs-grm and @fig-raw-mean-vs-theta. Over all 3668 products, raw mean ratings and GRM scores correlated at 0.906 (Pearson) and 0.932 (Spearman). The mean absolute shift in percentile rank was 0.080, a share of 0.350 of products changed quintile, and a share of 0.022 changed by two or more quintiles. Among products with the same raw mean, the GRM scores lay on average 0.814 and at most 2.252 apart. By number of ratings, the correlations were highest and the share of products changing quintile lowest for products with three or more ratings (Pearson 0.954, Spearman 0.959; share changing quintile 0.266), compared with products with one rating (0.921, 0.940; 0.385) and two ratings (0.922, 0.933; 0.319). @fig-raw-mean-vs-theta shows the vertical spread of GRM scores at a given raw mean; the points are jittered horizontally.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-raw-mean-vs-grm >}}

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#fig-raw-mean-vs-theta >}}

The consequences of constraining rater differences are shown in @tbl-score-agreement. Relative to the GRM, the scores of M1 correlated at 0.975 (Pearson) and 0.978 (Spearman), with a mean absolute percentile shift of 0.042; a share of 0.202 of products changed quintile and 0.004 changed by two or more quintiles. For M2, the corresponding values were 0.985, 0.983, 0.033, 0.150 and 0.003, and for M3 0.996, 0.996, 0.017, 0.075 and 0.001. Among the ladder models, Pearson correlations ranged from 0.980 to 0.993 and Spearman correlations from 0.983 to 0.996 (@tbl-theta-correlations). M1 re-estimated with the default integration grid correlated at 1.000 with M1. Comparing the two tables, the share of products changing quintile was higher for the raw mean (0.350) than for any of the IRT models relative to the GRM (at most 0.202), and the correlations of the raw mean with the GRM scores were lower than every correlation between models.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-score-agreement >}}

No confidence intervals are available for these correlations, agreement statistics and raw-mean comparisons. Moreover, the contrast between M1 and the GRM combines the rater constraints with a change of link function, whereas M3 and the GRM have the same number of parameters and differ only in the link. With these qualifications, scoring products by their raw mean changed the ranking more than any of the model constraints did, and constraining raters to equivalence changed it more than the choice of link function did. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-10\]]{.mark}

## Sensitivity to the rater exclusion

Refitting the GRM with all 22 raters (7844 ratings, 3669 products) changed the empirical marginal reliability from 0.67199 to 0.67186 and the model-based marginal reliability from 0.95986 to 0.96186 (@tbl-sensitivity-rater-exclusion). Over the 3668 common products, the scores of the two fits correlated at 0.99997 (Pearson) and 0.99996 (Spearman); the mean absolute difference was 0.00171, the maximum 0.16246, and a share of 0.00491 of products changed quintile. Over the 19 common raters, the discriminations correlated at 0.99880, with a maximum absolute difference of 0.19820. No confidence intervals are available for these differences.

# Discussion

This study set out to describe how the reliability of creativity scores for football actions depends on the number of ratings, how raters differ, and whether these differences need to be modelled. The reliability of the obtained scores rose with the number of ratings per product and stayed below that of a hypothetical full panel. Raters differed in severity, scale use, discrimination and information. The constraints that treat raters as equivalent were rejected by the LR tests and AIC, although BIC did not favour rater-specific discriminations. Both raw mean scoring and the choice of a constrained model shifted the ranking of products, raw mean scoring most. These results rest on the GRM, which described the ratings best by all information criteria.

## How many ratings per action? Reliability of the scores actually used

The conventional figures describe the mean of a large or complete panel. The full-panel reliability (0.960) and the pairwise Cronbach's alpha (0.928) both lie in the range that CAT studies usually report. The scores that were actually obtained, however, had an empirical reliability of 0.672 [0.649, 0.687], and this is the figure that matters for any downstream use of the scores. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-3\]]{.mark} This difference follows the Spearman–Brown logic described by @amabile1982: reliability depends on the number of ratings that are aggregated, and the panel coefficients refer to more ratings per product than the products actually received. The contrast between Krippendorff's alpha for single ratings (0.392) and the pairwise Cronbach's alpha (0.928) illustrates the point made by @kaufman2008 that a high alpha can hide low agreement between individual raters. The alpha on the fully crossed block (0.658, three raters) lay close to the empirical reliability, although the two indices refer to different quantities and this closeness should not be read as equivalence. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-13\]]{.mark}

The results by number of ratings provide first football-specific evidence on the question raised by @cseh2019 of how many ratings a domain requires. Product-level precision depended mainly on the number of ratings, but products with the same number of ratings still differed. A likely reason is that precision also depends on where a product lies relative to its raters' thresholds (@fig-grm-rel-post-by-theta), which is consistent with the finding that raters provide information in different regions of $\theta$; precision therefore also depends on which raters rated a product. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-4: the comparison across numbers of ratings is observational\]]{.mark} For reporting, this implies that creativity studies should report the reliability of the scores actually used, that is, the empirical marginal reliability and product standard errors, and not only alpha or full-panel values. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-15\]]{.mark}

## Raters differ

The raters spanned a wide range of severity, scale use and discrimination. Their first thresholds, threshold spacing, floor rates and central rates differed markedly, and for raters with many ratings the differences in discrimination clearly exceeded the standard errors, for example between R09 (0.863, *SE* 0.151) and R06 (2.807, *SE* 0.424). [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-6\]]{.mark} These differences are in line with reports of differing scale use and beliefs about creativity among CAT raters [@long2015] and with the rater effects described in rater-mediated assessment, such as severity, central tendency and restriction of range [@engelhard1994; @myford2003; @myford2004]. The contrast between raters who concentrated their ratings in the middle categories (e.g., R13) and raters who used the floor category heavily (e.g., R06) corresponds to the preference for central or extreme categories discussed by @myszkowski2021. @primi2019 left such interactions between raters and the rating scale to future research; the present results describe them for ratings of football actions. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-6\]]{.mark}

The uncertainty of these estimates needs to be considered. For the raters with about 50 ratings, R16 and R19, the highest discriminations and information shares came with the widest intervals. The information shares are therefore not a ranking of rater quality. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-12\]]{.mark} This is consistent with work showing that rater estimates in incomplete rating networks depend on the size of the linking set [@wind2018; @wind2019a] and that GRM parameter recovery requires adequate numbers of responses [@reise1990]. Which rater characteristics predict discernment is a separate question [@ceh2022]. Finally, raters informed different regions of the latent scale: R06 was most informative at high creativity, with their maximum information at $\theta$ = 2.400 and a share of only 0.001 at $\theta = -2$, whereas R12 contributed the largest share at $\theta = -2$ (0.221). This is relevant for assigning raters to products. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-16\]]{.mark}

## Why rater differences need to be modelled in creativity research in sport

Unweighted means and coefficient alpha assume $\tau$-equivalent raters [@myszkowski2019]. The LR tests rejected even the weaker constraints of the Rasch family, a shared category structure and equal discrimination. Averaging therefore treats raters as interchangeable when they are not, and whenever different raters rate different actions, the severity of the assigned raters is confounded with the score [@primi2019]. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-7\]]{.mark}

The comparison of raw means with model-based scores shows this consequence directly. The raw mean moved a share of 0.350 of products to another quintile relative to the GRM score, more than any IRT model did (0.202 at most), and products with the same raw mean received GRM scores up to 2.252 apart. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-22\]]{.mark} A plausible mechanism is that products with the same raw mean get different GRM scores when they were rated by raters of different severity or discrimination. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-21: this is the explanation given in the analysis notebook, not a tested result\]]{.mark} Agreement between raw means and GRM scores was higher, and fewer products changed quintile, for products with three or more ratings than for products with one or two. A cautious reading is that with more ratings per product, the differences between individual raters weigh less in the mean; the groups were not compared by a statistical test. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-22\]]{.mark} These results agree with the observation of @primi2019 that means are confounded with rater severity in incomplete designs, and with the argument of @myszkowski2019 against the assumption of $\tau$-equivalence.

Rater-specific discriminations were supported by the LR test and AIC, but not by BIC. Part of the observed heterogeneity in discrimination may be estimation noise for raters with few ratings, whose standard errors were largest under both M3 and the GRM. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-7\]]{.mark} The fit of the raters under M1 is consistent with the account that the MFRM expresses differences in discrimination only as misfit [@myford2004; @myszkowski2021]. R17, the rater with the highest infit and outfit values under M1, had a comparatively low GRM discrimination (1.446), whereas R12, the rater with the lowest values under M1, had a high GRM discrimination (2.898). Because no cut-offs were applied, this pattern describes values above and below 1 rather than misfitting raters. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-9\]]{.mark}

The GRM was preferred by all information criteria. A cumulative link is plausible for a unipolar creativity scale, and @pellegrino2025 also retained a GRM for creativity ratings. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-8\]]{.mark} Neither the unordered steps in M2 and M3 nor the ordered GRM thresholds count as evidence for either family, because unordered steps in adjacent-category models indicate only that some category is never the most likely response [@andrich1978; @bond2020], and GRM thresholds are ordered by construction. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-9\]]{.mark}

The choice of scoring model also mattered. Although all correlations between models were 0.975 or higher, a share of 0.202 of products changed quintile between the MFRM/RSM and the GRM, and 0.075 between the GPCM and the GRM. For applications that select or label actions, for example, the top quintile of creative actions for training purposes or labels for automated rating, such shifts matter, and the shifts caused by raw mean scoring matter most. Because the MFRM–GRM contrast combines the rater constraints with a change of link function, the two sources cannot be separated in this comparison. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-10\]]{.mark}

## Practical implications for creativity research in sport

The results suggest four implications for the design and scoring of creativity ratings in sport. First, the number of ratings per action can be planned for a target score reliability. @tbl-grm-reliability-by-n shows the mean product-level reliability that products with a given number of ratings reached in this study; for example, products with four ratings had a mean rel~post~ of 0.810. These values refer to this rater pool and this scale, involve no extrapolation, and will be refined as more ratings are collected. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-5\]]{.mark}

Second, a calibration set of actions rated by all raters would link the raters, make their parameters comparable and stabilise the discriminations of raters with few ratings [@wind2019a; @forthmann2023]; it would also make fully crossed reliability and global fit statistics estimable. Such a calibration set is distinct from rater training, which conflicts with the CAT rule of independent judgement without imposed criteria [@hennessey2011; @dollinger2005; @storme2014]. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-14\]]{.mark}

Third, rater differences should be modelled rather than averaged. JRT scores with their posterior standard deviations can replace raw means; the raw-mean comparison is direct evidence that this choice changes which actions rank high. The empirical marginal reliability and the product standard errors should be reported and carried into downstream analyses. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-15, ATC-22\]]{.mark}

Fourth, rater workload and assignment deserve planning. The exclusion cut-off of 15 ratings is a minimum, and raters with about 50 ratings still had wide intervals for discrimination and information. Rater information functions could additionally inform the assignment of raters to actions. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-16\]]{.mark}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Design recommendations for creativity ratings in sport"}
1. Plan the number of ratings per action from the reliability you need, and report it (see @tbl-grm-reliability-by-n). [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-23, ATC-5\]]{.mark}
2. Let all raters rate a common calibration set of actions, so that raters are linked and their parameters are comparable. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-23, ATC-14\]]{.mark}
3. Give each rater enough ratings for stable rater parameters; 15 ratings is a lower limit, not a target (see @tbl-grm-rater-parameters and @tbl-grm-rater-information-ci). [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-23, ATC-16\]]{.mark}
4. Score actions with a judge response theory model rather than the raw mean rating (see @tbl-raw-mean-vs-grm). [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-23, ATC-15, ATC-22\]]{.mark}
5. Report the reliability of the scores actually used (empirical marginal reliability, product standard errors), not only alpha or full-panel values (see @tbl-reliability-overview). [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-23, ATC-3, ATC-15\]]{.mark}
:::

## Limitations and future research

Several limitations qualify these results. First, the rating design was incomplete: not every rater rated every product, and the analysis assumes that the missing ratings are ignorable given the allocation of products to raters. [\[FILL IN: allocation procedure (FI-4)\]]{.mark} The comparison across numbers of ratings is observational, and the cells with many ratings are small. The additional ratings that are being collected will strengthen this comparison.

Second, the fit evidence is limited by the design. S-X² is conservative because most cells are imputed; C2 could not be computed because some rater pairs share no products; Q3 is negatively biased when few raters rate each product [@christensen2017]; and infit and outfit values below 1 are expected when each product's score is estimated from the same few ratings. The absence of detected misfit is therefore not evidence of fit. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-11\]]{.mark} A calibration set rated by all raters would make these checks considerably more informative.

Third, the parameters of raters with few ratings are uncertain, and the response-style indices are raw descriptives without uncertainty. Fourth, the raters formed a single pool of students, and no rater covariates were analysed. [\[FILL IN: rater pool characteristics (FI-1)\]]{.mark} The role of expertise was outside the scope of this paper and remains a question for future work [@kaufman2009; @kaufman2013; @ceh2022]. Fifth, raters with fewer than 15 ratings were excluded; excluding them did not change the scores (@tbl-sensitivity-rater-exclusion).

Sixth, the model comparison has caveats: the M1–M2 test compares models estimated in different software, and its degrees of freedom are below the formula value because of unused end categories; BIC disagreed with the LR test and AIC on discrimination; the score-agreement contrasts mix rater constraints and link function; and the raw-mean comparison has no confidence intervals, and its grouping definitions remain to be documented. Seventh, the models included two facets and one dimension only. They contain no facet for time, session or fatigue, although rater tendencies can drift [@barth2020; @leckie2011; @myford2009] and workload affects agreement [@forthmann2017], and they do not test differential rater functioning [@wind2019b]. Rater models with additional structure, such as the hierarchical rater model [@patz2002] or generalized many-facet models [@uto2020], could address these extensions. Unidimensionality was assumed, and only the creativity dimension was analysed.

Future work should therefore use a prospective design with a calibration set rated by all raters, plan the number of ratings per action by simulation or a decision study [@forthmann2023], include rater covariates, and replicate the analysis in other sports.

# Conclusion

We have shown, for creativity ratings of football actions, that the reliability of the scores depends on the number of ratings per action and that the reliability of the scores actually obtained is far below the figures conventionally reported for a full panel. Raters differed in severity, scale use, discrimination and information. Treating raters as equivalent was rejected, and both raw mean scoring and constrained models shifted the ranking of actions. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-1\]]{.mark} Creativity research in sport should therefore plan the number of ratings per action, link raters through a common calibration set, and model rater differences with judge response theory instead of averaging ratings. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-5, ATC-14, ATC-15\]]{.mark}
